paper_a.title: The sphere packing problem in dimension 8

paper_b.title: The sphere packing problem in dimension 24

metadata.description: Paper B (Cohn-Kumar-Miller-Radchenko-Viazovska, d=24) directly extends paper A (Viazovska, d=8) by transporting the modular-form magic-function construction from the E8 lattice to the Leech lattice. The two proofs share a near-identical skeleton: Cohn-Elkies LP bound, +1 and -1 radial Fourier eigenfunctions a(r), b(r) built as contour integrals against (quasi)modular forms, contour-deformation/double-zero arguments, and a final A(t)<0 / B(t)>0 verification. Paper B replaces auxiliary forms (φ_{-2}, φ_{-4}, h, ψ_I) by a quasimodular weight-(-8) form φ and a weight-(-10) modular form ψ_I for Γ(2), and replaces interval-arithmetic with Sturm-on-truncated-q-series in PARI/GP.

matches.explanation: Both papers define a sphere packing in R^d as a discrete set of unit balls with disjoint interiors. Paper B splits the notion across two definitions (general density + lattice/periodic packings); paper A defines the packing object itself. Mathematically the same objects.

The packing density Delta_P and the sphere packing constant Delta_d in paper A correspond to the 'fraction of R^n covered' and the 'maximal density' notions in paper B's single density definition. Identical mathematical content.
Both papers use the standard Fourier transform with normalization $\widehat{f}(y)=\int f(x) e^{-2\pi i x\cdot y}dx$.
Schwartz function definition is auxiliary/external in paper A. Paper B takes Schwartz space as background without an explicit definition node.

Paper A's notions of admissible function and Cohn-Elkies-optimal function are paper-specific organizational definitions; paper B works directly with Schwartz functions and inlines the Cohn-Elkies hypotheses into Theorem TP401.2 without separate admissibility/optimality definitions.

Paper A's E_8 lattice has no analogue node in paper B; paper B's optimal lattice is the Leech lattice, mentioned implicitly in TP401.1 but not given an explicit definition node. The E_8 vs Leech distinction is the core extension going from d=8 to d=24.

Both define the slash operator / automorphy factor for SL_2(Z)-action on the upper half plane. Paper A separates the modular group definition from the slash operator; paper B states only the slash operator. Same classical material.
Paper A explicitly defines holomorphic and weakly-holomorphic modular forms; paper B uses these notions implicitly via citations and does not introduce the corresponding nodes.
Both define the weight-k Eisenstein series E_k with the same Fourier expansion in terms of sigma_{k-1}(n). Identical classical objects.

The quasimodular form E_2 is an explicit definition in paper A; paper B folds it into the unified Eisenstein-series definition DP401.4 (mentioning that E_k for k=2 is quasimodular). Same classical object.
Both papers define the three theta-nullwerte Theta_{00}, Theta_{01}, Theta_{10} with identical formulas; paper B even cites paper A. Same definition.

Paper A states Jacobi's identity Theta_{01}^4+Theta_{10}^4=Theta_{00}^4 as a separate equation node; paper B includes the same identity inside the theta-functions definition node DP401.8. Same classical identity.

Paper A defines the j-invariant j=1728 E_4^3/(E_4^3-E_6^2); paper B defines the modular discriminant Delta=(E_4^3-E_6^2)/1728. The two are reciprocals of one another in numerator-denominator, both the standard 'normalising' weight-12 / weight-0 generators of the ring of modular forms for SL_2(Z); they play closely related roles even though they are not the same object.

Paper A's auxiliary modular forms phi_{-2}, phi_{-4} and the depth-2 quasimodular triple phi_{-4}, phi_{-2}, phi_0 (built from E_4, E_6, j and E_2) are the d=8 analogue of paper B's single quasimodular form phi (built from E_4, E_6, E_2, Delta) of weight -8 and depth 2. Same role (the +1-eigenfunction modular ingredient), different weight (-4 family vs -8) reflecting the dimension change 8 to 24.

Both define the +1 radial Fourier eigenfunction a(r) as a contour integral against the auxiliary (quasi)modular form. In d=8 the integrand involves phi_0 with weight z^2; in d=24 it involves phi with weight z^{10}. The role and the contour structure are identical; the weight, lattice scale (length sqrt(2) vs 2), and the specific modular form differ to match the dimension.

Paper A's auxiliary form h on Gamma_0(2) (used to build psi_I) does not appear as a separate node in paper B; paper B writes psi_I directly as a quotient of theta-powers and Delta^2 without intermediate h.

Paper A defines psi_I, psi_T, psi_S in d=8 as h-h|_{-2}ST, psi_I|_{-2}T, psi_I|_{-2}S of weight -2 for Gamma_0(2). Paper B introduces psi_I, psi_S, psi_T of weight -10 for Gamma(2), as theta-power expressions, with psi_S=psi_I|_{-10}S, psi_T=psi_I|_{-10}T. Same role (the -1 eigenfunction modular ingredient) and same structural identity psi_S+psi_T=psi_I; different weight and ambient subgroup reflecting the dimension change.
Both define the -1 radial Fourier eigenfunction b(r) as a contour integral involving psi_I (or psi_T, psi_S). Paper A uses weight -2; paper B uses weight -10. Identical role, different weight.

Paper B defines a single optimal auxiliary function f as a linear combination of a and b with specific rational coefficients; paper A defines the same kind of object inside Theorem TP400.4 (g = (pi i / 8640) a + (i / 240 pi) b) without isolating it as a separate definition node. The matching node on side A is the construction theorem TP400.4.

Paper B defines auxiliary kernels A(t), B(t) for f, fhat as integral kernels. Paper A introduces the same kernels A(t), B(t) only inline within proof steps PSP400.14 and PSP400.18 (proof of TP400.4 / PP400.8). Same kernels, different node-level granularity.

Both are the main theorem: optimal sphere packing density is achieved by E_8 in d=8 (Delta_8 = pi^4/384) vs by Leech in d=24 (Delta_24 = pi^12/12!). Same statement structure, parallel result, different dimension and lattice. Paper B additionally asserts uniqueness of the optimal periodic packing up to scaling/isometries.
Both papers cite the Cohn-Elkies linear programming bound (Cohn-Elkies, Annals 2003) as their starting tool. Identical theorem; both nodes have origin=external with the same citation.

Paper B's TP401.3 is exactly Viazovska's d=8 result (paper A's main theorem TP400.1) cited as prior work. This is the strongest single signal that the relation is EXT: paper B explicitly cites paper A's main contribution.

Paper A's remark RP400.1 invokes Cohn-Elkies Conjecture 8.1 to conclude E_8 is the unique densest periodic packing in d=8. Paper B's TP401.4 is the Cohn-Elkies uniqueness criterion specialised to d=24 (used to deduce Leech is unique optimal periodic packing). Same conceptual role, both citing Section 8 of Cohn-Elkies.

Paper A states the existence of a magic Schwartz function g as an intermediate theorem TP400.3, then proves it via TP400.4 (explicit construction). Paper B does not have a separate existence theorem; LP401.1 + LP401.2 + DP401.12 + PP401.3 collectively serve the same purpose. The closest match is the construction PP401.3, but at the theorem level there is no exact analogue.

Paper A's TP400.4 explicitly constructs g = (pi i / 8640) a + (i / 240 pi) b and verifies the LP-bound conditions. Paper B encodes the same step partly as the definition DP401.12 (f = -(pi i / 113218560) a - (i / 262080 pi) b) and partly as the proof PP401.3 (verification of Cohn-Elkies hypotheses). Identical structural step with different rational coefficients reflecting d=24.

Both establish that a is a Schwartz function and a +1 radial Fourier eigenfunction (a-hat = a). Paper A frames it as a proposition about a defined by the four-piece contour integral; paper B as a lemma about a defined by a single contour integral with a sin^2 prefactor. Same statement modulo dimension.

Paper A's Proposition PrP400.2 (a has double zeroes at lattice points of length > sqrt(2), with explicit single-integral formula) is a separate intermediate proposition. Paper B incorporates the analogous fact directly into the definition DP401.10 of a(r) for r>2 and uses it inline in PP401.3 step PSP401.12 without a separate proposition node.

Paper A's PrP400.3 gives an alternative integral representation of a(r) valid on [0,infinity) by subtracting the asymptotic part. Paper B's EP401.3 states the same kind of closed-form for a(r), with the asymptotic polynomial p(t) (paper B EP401.2) playing the role of the explicit terms in PrP400.3. Same role, different weight/normalisation.

Paper A's PrP400.4 lists special values of a (a(0), a(sqrt(2)), a'(sqrt(2))). Paper B verifies the analogous special values inside step PSP401.11 of PP401.3 without isolating them as a proposition. The values themselves differ (different scale).

Both establish that b is a Schwartz function and a -1 radial Fourier eigenfunction (b-hat = -b). Paper A as a proposition with the four-piece definition, paper B as a lemma with the single-integral / sin^2 form.

Paper A's PrP400.6 (b has double zeroes at lattice points of length > sqrt(2), single-integral formula) is folded into paper B's definition DP401.11 of b for r>2; no standalone proposition in paper B.

Paper A's PrP400.7 gives an alternative integral representation for b(r) valid on [0,infinity); paper B's EP401.4 states an analogous closed-form with subtracted asymptotic exponential terms. Identical structural role.
Special values of b at 0 and sqrt(2). Paper B verifies analogous values inline in PSP401.11 without a separate proposition.
Poisson summation for E_8: an external/classical input applied to Lambda_8. Paper B uses Poisson summation only implicitly (subsumed in the citation of Cohn-Elkies); no corresponding equation node.

The phi_0 transformation rule under z -> -1/z in paper A and the quasimodularity relation z^8 phi(-1/z) = phi(z) + phi_1/z + phi_2/z^2 in paper B play the same role: they encode how the +1-eigenfunction modular form transforms under the involution that drives the contour-deformation argument. Different weights match the dimensions.

The identity psi_T + psi_S = psi_I in paper A is an explicit equation node; paper B uses the same identity inline in PSP401.8 (psi_T - psi_I = -psi_S) without a separate equation node. Same identity, different node-level granularity.

The Gaussian Fourier transform identity in dimension 8 is an external classical input in paper A. Paper B uses the d=24 version z^{-12} e^{pi i r^2 (-1/z)} inline in PSP401.5 / PSP401.9 without a separate equation node.

Paper B's EP401.2 (asymptotics of t^{10} phi(i/t) as t->infty, polynomial p(t) up to O(t^2 e^{-2 pi t})) is the d=24 analogue of paper A's asymptotic terms used inside PrP400.3 / PSP400.15. No standalone equation node on side A.

Paper B explicitly factors out f(r) = sin^2(pi r^2/2) integral_0^infty A(t) e^{-pi r^2 t} dt and similarly for fhat. Paper A uses the same factorisation but only inline within proof steps PSP400.14 / PSP400.18; not isolated as separate equation nodes.

Both proofs establish a-hat = a using the same skeleton: estimate a as Schwartz via a Bessel/exponential bound, exchange the contour integral with the Fourier transform via the Gaussian formula, change variables w=-1/z, apply the transformation rule for the +1-eigenfunction modular form. Paper A's modular form is phi_0 (weight 0), paper B's is phi (weight -8); the d=8 vs d=24 dimension shows up in the Gaussian formula's z-power (z^{-4} vs z^{-12}).

Composite L2 alignment of the proof steps inside PP400.1 / PP401.1 (proofs of a-hat = a). Paper A's three steps (Bessel K_1 estimate; exchange contour and Fourier; substitute w=-1/z and use 1-periodicity) correspond to paper B's six finer-grained steps (trig identity; contour shift; quasimodularity; analytic continuation/Schwartz decay; 24-D radial Fourier; w=-1/z change of variable). Paper B unrolls the identity step into a Lemma-style sub-argument (LP401.6), reflecting the more involved depth-2 quasimodular setting.
Paper A's proof of double zeroes of a (PP400.2) is folded into paper B's reduction step PSP401.12 (f(r) <= 0 reduces to A(t) <= 0 via the integral representation), without a separate proof node.
Paper A's proof of the alternative integral representation of a (PP400.3) is encoded in paper B as the asymptotics expansion EP401.2 + EP401.3, not as a separate proof node.
Paper A's proof of special values of a (direct evaluation of the integral representation) has no dedicated proof-node analogue in paper B; the corresponding values are computed inline in PSP401.11.

Both proofs establish b-hat = -b by Bessel-style Schwartz bound; exchange of contour and Fourier integration; change of variables; application of the slash-operator identities psi_T|_k S = -psi_T, psi_I|_k S = psi_S, psi_S|_k S = psi_I. Identical proof skeleton; weight is k=-2 (paper A) vs k=-10 (paper B).

Composite L2 alignment of proof steps inside PP400.5 / PP401.2 (proofs of b-hat = -b). Paper A's three steps (Bessel K_1 bound; exchange contour+Fourier; apply slash identities) match paper B's four steps (substitute trig + shift contours; apply psi_T-psi_I=-psi_S; 24-D Fourier and change variables; conclude via psi_I|S=psi_S etc.). Granularity differs but the substantive content is the same.

Paper A's proof of double zeroes of b (PP400.6, including verification of psi_T+psi_S=psi_I via group-theoretic manipulations in Gamma_0(2)) is folded in paper B into the definition DP401.9 (asserting the linear relation as part of the construction) and used inline in PSP401.8.
Paper A's proof of alternative integral representation of b mirrors PP400.3's role for a; paper B does not isolate this as a proof node, encoding it instead in EP401.4.

Both are the master proof of the construction theorem: define f (or g) as a specific linear combination of a and b; reduce f<=0 / fhat>=0 to inequalities A(t)<0 / B(t)>0 on the kernel functions; verify normalisation f(0)=fhat(0)=1. Paper A verifies A(t)<0 and B(t)>0 by interval-arithmetic on truncated asymptotic expansions; paper B reduces them to the standalone Lemmas LP401.3, LP401.4, LP401.5 proved in Appendix A by Sturm's theorem on truncated q-series. Same proof architecture, different verification machinery.

Composite L2 alignment of proof steps inside PP400.8 / PP401.3 (master construction proof). Paper A's seven steps (reduce g<=0 to A(t)<0; compute asymptotics A_0^(6), A_inf^(6); Bruinier coefficient bounds; interval-arithmetic; reduce ghat>=0 to B(t)>0; interval-arithmetic for B; verify g(0)=ghat(0)=1) align with paper B's six steps (define f and verify normalisation/root structure; reduce f<=0 to A<=0; reduce A<=0 to varphi(it)<=0; show fhat>=0 on [sqrt 2,inf); handle fhat>=0 on (0,sqrt 2); apply Cohn-Elkies bound and uniqueness). The crucial technical difference: paper B outsources sign-verification to Appendix-A Sturm-PARI/GP lemmas, whereas paper A inlines interval-arithmetic with explicit truncation and Bruinier-style Fourier-coefficient bounds.

Paper A's PP400.9 is the short final proof of the main theorem (apply Cohn-Elkies to f(x)=g(sqrt(2)x); read off Delta_8 <= pi^4/384). Paper B folds this final step into the same proof PP401.3 (which already contains the Cohn-Elkies application + uniqueness via TP401.4). PP401.3 thus matches both PP400.8 (construction) and PP400.9 (closing argument).

Paper A's two closing steps (set f(x)=g(sqrt(2)x) and apply Cohn-Elkies; read off Delta_8 <= pi^4/384) collapse into paper B's single closing step PSP401.16 (apply Cohn-Elkies bound and the uniqueness criterion of CE). Same conclusion, different rescaling factor (sqrt(2) vs 2).

Paper A's remark on forced double zeroes from Poisson summation motivating the integral-transform construction has no dedicated node in paper B. The same observation drives paper B's construction but is not stated as a remark.

Paper B's remarks on the ansatz for phi (5-dimensional space of weight-16 quasimodular forms of depth 2) and the ansatz for psi_I (8-dimensional space of weight-14 modular forms for Gamma(2)) describe the explicit search space pinning down the magic functions. Paper A does not include such ansatz remarks.

Paper B's remark on Cohn-Miller numerical conjectures specifically references conjectured special values that paper B's f, fhat are shown to satisfy; this is a paper-B-specific contribution with no analogue in paper A (which predates Cohn-Miller-style numerics for the d=24 case).
Both papers state the sphere packing problem in their respective dimension as the driving problem. Identical role; different dimension.

Lemma LP401.3 (varphi(it)<0 for all t>0) is a paper-B-specific computer-algebra-verified inequality, used inside PP401.3. Paper A's analogue is not isolated as a lemma but inlined inside PSP400.14-PSP400.17 with interval-arithmetic; we record this as none rather than analogous because the lemma packaging is genuinely paper-B-specific.
Lemma LP401.4 (varphi - (432/pi^2) psi_S > 0) is a paper-B-specific computer-algebra-verified inequality used to bound A(t). No standalone-lemma analogue in paper A.
Lemma LP401.5 (leading-term lower bound on B(t) for t>=1) is paper-B-specific. Paper A's analogous bound on B(t) is inlined inside PSP400.18-PSP400.19 without a standalone lemma.

Paper B's Sinkhorn-style identity (LP401.6: phi(-1/(z+1))(z+1)^{10} - 2 phi(-1/z) z^{10} + phi(-1/(z-1))(z-1)^{10} = 2 phi(z)) is the d=24 analogue of paper A's identity inside PSP400.6 (phi_0(-1/(z+1))(z+1)^2 - 2 phi_0(-1/z) z^2 + phi_0(-1/(z-1))(z-1)^2 = 2 phi_0(z)). Same identity, different weight; paper B isolates it as a lemma, paper A inlines it.

Paper B introduces the Sturm-on-truncated-q-series algorithm (AP401.1) as a reusable computer-algebra-verification procedure. Paper A's verification uses a different, ad-hoc interval-arithmetic + Bruinier-coefficient-bound procedure (PSP400.16, PSP400.17, PSP400.19), inlined in proof steps and not packaged as an algorithm node. This is a substantive difference between the two proofs.
